prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My heart is a-breaking, dear Tittie, Some counsel unto me come len'; To anger them a' is a pity, But what will I do wi' Tam Glen? I'm thinking, wi' sic a braw fellow, In poortith I might mak a fen': What care I in riches to wallow, If I mauna marry Tam Glen? There's Lowrie, the laird o' Dumeller, "Guid-day to you,"—brute! he comes ben: He brags and he blaws o' his siller, But when will he dance like Tam Glen? My minnie does constantly deave me, And bids me beware o' young men; They flatter, she says, to deceive me; But wha can think sae o' Tam Glen? My daddie says, gin I'll forsake him, He'll gie me guid hunder marks ten: But, if it's ordain'd I maun take him, O wha will I get but Tam Glen? Yestreen at the valentines' dealing, My heart to my mou gied a sten: For thrice I drew ane without failing, And thrice it was written, "Tam Glen"! The last Halloween I was waukin My droukit sark-sleeve, as ye ken: His likeness cam up the house staukin, And the very gray breeks o' Tam Glen! Come counsel, dear Tittie, don't tarry; I'll gie ye my bonie black hen, Gif ye will advise me to marry The lad I lo'e dearly, Tam Glen.

outputs.L1:
My heart is a-breaking, dear Tittie;  
Some counsel unto me come len’.  
To anger them a’ is a pity—  
But what will I do wi’ Tam Glen?

I’m thinking, wi’ sic a braw fellow,  
In poortith I might mak a fen’.  
What care I in riches to wallow,  
If I mauna marry Tam Glen?

There’s Lowrie, the laird o’ Dumeller—  
“Guid day to you!”—brute! He comes ben.  
He brags and he blaws o’ his siller,  
But when will he dance like Tam Glen?

My minnie does constantly deave me  
And bids me beware o’ young men.  
“They flatter,” she says, “to deceive me”;  
But wha can think sae o’ Tam Glen?

My daddie says, gin I’ll forsake him,  
He’ll gie me guid hunder marks ten;  
But if it’s ordain’d I maun take him,  
O wha will I get but Tam Glen?

Yestreen, at the valentines’ dealing,  
My heart to my mou gied a sten;  
For thrice I drew ane without failing,  
And thrice it was written: “Tam Glen!”

The last Halloween, I was waukin  
My droukit sark-sleeve, as ye ken;  
His likeness cam up the house staukin—  
And the very gray breeks o’ Tam Glen!

Come counsel, dear Tittie; don’t tarry.  
I’ll gie ye my bonie black hen,  
Gif ye will advise me to marry  
The lad I lo’e dearly—Tam Glen.
outputs.L2:
Dear sister, my heart is nearly shattered,  
So please offer me some advice.  
I hate the thought of upsetting everyone,  
Yet what am I to do about Tam Glen?

With such a fine man beside me,  
I believe I could manage even in poverty.  
Why should I care about living in wealth  
If I am forbidden to marry Tam Glen?

Then there is Lowrie, the lord of Dumeller.  
The brute strolls inside with his formal greeting,  
Boasting loudly about all his money—  
But could he ever dance as Tam Glen does?

Mother never stops lecturing me,  
Warning me to be cautious of young men.  
She claims they use flattery to mislead women,  
But who could suspect Tam Glen of such a thing?

Father promises that if I give Tam up,  
He will pay me a full thousand marks.  
But if fate has decreed that I must marry,  
Who else could my husband be but Tam Glen?

Last night, while we were drawing valentines,  
My heart suddenly leapt into my mouth.  
Three separate times I chose a name,  
And every time it read, “Tam Glen.”

And last Halloween, as you already know,  
I kept watch over my soaked shirt-sleeve.  
A figure just like him came striding through the house,  
Even wearing Tam Glen’s very gray breeches.

Come quickly, dear sister, and tell me what to do.  
I will reward you with my lovely black hen  
If only you advise me to marry  
The young man I love so dearly—Tam Glen.
outputs.L3:
The speaker turns to her sister for advice because she is deeply in love with Tam Glen, even though her family and others disapprove of the match. Her feelings are unwavering: she would rather marry Tam than gain wealth or social status. She dismisses a rich, boastful suitor, insisting that all his money and pride cannot make him equal to the man she truly loves.

Her parents try to persuade her to change her mind. Her mother warns that young men are often deceitful and unreliable, while her father offers her a substantial sum of money if she will abandon Tam Glen. Nevertheless, the speaker remains convinced that Tam is the right man for her. Traditional Valentine’s Day and Halloween divinations repeatedly seem to reveal him as her destined partner, strengthening her belief that they are meant to be together.

In the end, she playfully offers her sister a prized hen in return for the advice she longs to hear: that she should ignore wealth, family pressure, and social disapproval and marry the man she loves.
outputs.L4:
### Tam Glen

“My heart is nearly breaking, dear sister,” the young woman confessed. “Please, lend me your counsel. I hate to anger the whole family, but what am I to do about Tam Glen?”

She knew Tam was not wealthy. If she married him, they might have to live modestly and work hard to make ends meet. Yet he was handsome, lively, and good-hearted, and she believed she could endure poverty beside him. What pleasure could she find in riches if she were forbidden to marry the man she loved?

There were wealthier suitors, of course. The laird of Dumeller often came calling, boasting endlessly of his land and silver. Her family considered him an excellent match, but she found him proud and tiresome. For all his money, he could never dance with Tam’s grace or bring her the same joy.

Her mother constantly warned her to be cautious. Young men, she said, were skilled at flattering women only to deceive them. But the young woman could not believe such suspicions of Tam. Whatever might be true of others, her heart told her that he was sincere.

Her father tried a different argument. He promised her a generous sum if she would give Tam up and choose someone more respectable. Still, she remained unmoved. If marriage was her destiny, she could imagine no husband but Tam Glen.

Even the old customs and omens seemed to confirm her choice. During the drawing of valentines, she reached into the lot three times. Each time, to her astonishment, she drew the same name: Tam Glen. At Halloween she tried another traditional charm, and a figure appeared just as Tam might have done, wearing even the same gray breeches.

“How can I ignore so many signs?” she asked her sister. “Do not keep me waiting. Tell me that I should marry him, and I will give you my beautiful black hen in gratitude. Wealth, family approval, and grand promises mean little to me beside the man I truly love. Whatever anyone else may say, my heart belongs to Tam Glen.”
outputs.L5: Tittie was an oddly named little bird with a bright red chest. Some people laughed when they heard her name, but she never seemed to mind. She simply sang louder, filling the garden with music and reminding everyone that confidence matters more than opinions.

In poortith I might mak a fen’;
